summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of how scientists measure earthquakes: a seismometer records ground shaking using a heavy mass that stays nearly still by inertia while the frame and paper move under it; earthquake energy spreads outward as waves that fade with distance; and a magnitude scale gives one number for an earthquake's strength, where each whole step up is a BIG jump: the recorded waves are roughly ten times bigger when compared at the same distance (not a linear notch), and much more energy is released. Keep the log idea intuitive, never computational. Core activity: a shakeable seismometer model with a live trace, a magnitude dial that visibly multiplies the wiggles, and a distance control that separates magnitude (the quake's true size) from how strongly a place feels it. Reference diagrams, quiz-based consolidation, and an optional 3D view are preserved as distinct supports.
misconceptions: The magnitude scale is linear (a 6 is only a bit more than a 5) — in fact each step is ~10× the shaking amplitude and far more energy.
A seismometer 'feels' the quake like a person (it works by a heavy mass staying still by inertia while the frame/ground moves).
Magnitude and how strongly you FEEL it are the same (magnitude is the source size; felt intensity depends on distance and ground).
Earthquake energy travels in straight lines to one place (it spreads outward as waves in all directions, fading with distance).
Bigger wiggles on the trace always mean a bigger earthquake regardless of distance (distance matters; scientists account for it).

activities.title: Shake a seismometer and read the trace
steps: Shake a model ground (physically with a weight hanging on a spring over a moving paper strip, or with an on-screen shake control) with quick, sharp shakes and watch the suspended heavy mass lag behind and stay nearly still while the frame and paper move under it (in a homemade model it may still swing or bob a little, and slow shakes can carry it along).
Watch the attached pen draw a live wiggly trace (a seismogram) and say in your own words why a mass that stays still can record motion: the GROUND and paper move, not the mass — that is inertia.
Shake harder and gentler and describe how the size (amplitude) of the wiggles changes: bigger wiggles mean stronger shaking.
Point to the parts and label them: the heavy mass (stays nearly still), the frame (moves with the ground), the pen, and the paper record.
activities.insight: A seismometer does not 'feel' a quake like a person; it works because a heavy suspended mass stays nearly still by inertia while everything else moves under it, tracing a record whose wiggle size shows how strong the shaking is.

activities.title: The magnitude staircase: each step is a big jump
steps: Before changing anything, predict: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5 — a little, or a lot?'

Keeping the seismometer at the same distance, turn a magnitude dial from 5 up to 6 (or use a visual step-staircase) and watch the trace amplitude leap roughly ten times bigger, with a released-energy meter jumping far more.
Step up again (6 to 7) and describe the pattern in words: each whole number means waves about ten times bigger on the trace (at the same distance), not 'one more'.
State the correction to a friend who says 'a 7 is just one more than a 6': no — measured at the same distance, a 7 makes waves about ten times bigger than a 6, and releases far more energy.
activities.insight: The magnitude scale is not like ordinary counting: each whole-number step means roughly ten times greater recorded wave amplitude when compared at the same distance (and much more energy released), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6.

activities.title: Same quake, different places: magnitude vs felt intensity
steps: With one fixed earthquake set, drag a distance control (or move a marker) to place a seismometer nearer and farther from the source, and watch the trace get smaller with distance.
Explain why people nearby feel the quake strongly while people far away barely notice it: the waves spread outward and fade with distance.
Answer: does moving farther away change the earthquake's MAGNITUDE, or only how strongly you FEEL it? (It changes only the felt intensity; magnitude is one fixed number for the quake.)
Connect to what you already know: the waves are the energy released when rocks snapped, spreading out in all directions from the source and shrinking as they go.
activities.insight: Magnitude is a single fixed number describing the earthquake's size at its source (from the energy released), while felt intensity depends on distance (and ground and buildings) and fades the farther away you are.

activities.title: Reference: label the seismometer and the seismogram
steps: Study a labelled seismometer cutaway and tap or point to each part: the suspended mass (reveal 'stays still — inertia'), the frame, the pen, the paper.
Examine an annotated seismogram and mark where the wiggles are biggest (largest amplitude = strongest shaking).
Open a 'Is a 6 just a bit more than a 5?' flap or note and read the ~10× reveal in your own words.
activities.insight: Naming the parts of a seismometer and reading amplitude on a seismogram gives a clear reference model that supports, but does not replace, the hands-on trace-building.

activities.title: Check and consolidate
steps: Order a set of seismograms from smallest to largest amplitude (weakest to strongest shaking).
Answer: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5?' and justify with the step-jump idea.

Respond to the two-part prompt: 'A friend says a magnitude 7 is just a little bit (about one) stronger than a 6 — is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you are on top of it or far away? Explain.'
activities.insight: A learner who has grasped the ideas can read traces by amplitude, state that each step is about ten times stronger, and separate the fixed magnitude from the distance-dependent felt intensity.

checkQuestion: A magnitude 7 earthquake and a magnitude 6 earthquake — a friend says 'the 7 is just a little bit stronger, about one more'. Is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you're right on top of it or far away? Explain.
checkAnswer: No — the scale isn't like ordinary counting. Each step up is about TEN times bigger shaking (and much more energy), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6, not 'one more'. And magnitude is a single number for the earthquake itself (from the energy released where the rocks broke) — it doesn't change with where you stand. What changes with distance is how strongly you FEEL it (the intensity), which fades the further away you are.
